parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -vout, from Old Dutch -falt, from Frankish *-fald, from Proto-Germanic *-faldaz.
From Middle Dutch bile, from Old Dutch and Frankish *billi, *bīal, *bīala, from Proto-Germanic *bilją (“axe”). Compare German Beil.
From Middle Dutch blōde, from Old Dutch *blōdi, from Frankish *blauthi, from Proto-Germanic *blauþuz (“weak”).
From Middle Dutch boele (“male relative”), further etymology unknown. May belong to Old Dutch and Frankish *buolo, from Proto-Germanic *bō- (“father, brother, close male relation”).
From Middle Dutch boorde, from Old Dutch *bordo, from Frankish *bord (“plank, board”), from Proto-Germanic *burdô, *burdą (“plank, board”).

From Middle Dutch *dronen, from Old Dutch *drunen, from Frankish *drunnjan; the long vowel /øː/ precludes a derivation from a hypothetical Proto-Germanic *drunjaną. Cognate to Middle Low German dronen, Old Norse drynja, and also related to Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌾𐌿𐍃 (drunjus).

From Middle Dutch else, from Old Dutch *alisa, from Frankish *alisu, from Proto-Germanic *alisō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élis-. Compare German Erle, English alder, Danish el, Norwegian older, Icelandic elri.

From Middle Dutch gevel, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Frankish *gebil, whence also Old High German gibil m (modern German Giebel) and gibilla f, meaning “gable”. Further cognates include Old Norse gafl (“gable”), Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌻𐌰 (gibla, “pinnacle, summit”) and Middle High German gebel (“skull”) (from O

parole.significato: brill, a fish of species Scophthalmus rhombus
parole.testo: Possibly from a word meaning "sandstone, grit," referring to the shingle seabed the fish resides on, from Middle Dutch griet, from Old Dutch *griot, from Frankish *greota, from Proto-Germanic *greutą.
From Middle Dutch comme, from Old Dutch *kumb, from Frankish *kumb, from Proto-Germanic *kumbaz.
From Middle Dutch crampe, from Old Dutch *crampo, from Frankish *krampa, from Proto-Germanic *krampô, related to *krampō.
From Middle Dutch cribbe, from Old Dutch kribba, from Frankish *kribbija, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Doublet of crèche.

parole.significato: stool (piece of furniture without back or armrests)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crucke, from Old Dutch *krukka, from Frankish *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō.
From Middle Dutch locke, from Old Dutch lock, from Frankish *lokk, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz.
From Middle Dutch and Old Dutch lot, from Frankish *hlot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.

parole.significato: a member of one's kin, a blood relative
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mâech, from Old Dutch *māg, from Frankish *māg, from Proto-Germanic *mēgaz. Cognate to German Mag, Gothic 𐌼𐌴𐌲𐍃 (mēgs, “son-in-law”), Swedish måg (“son-in-law”).

parole.significato: a raised earth mound, often topped with a wooden or stone structure and surrounded with a ditch; a motte
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mote, perhaps via Frankish *mot, *motta (“mud, peat, bog, turf”), from Proto-Germanic *mutô, *mudraz, *muþraz (“dirt, filth, mud, swamp”). Likely influenced by French motte.
From Middle Dutch mouwe, from Old Dutch *mouwa, *mōwa, from Frankish *mauwa, from Proto-Germanic *mawwō. Cognate with Central Franconian Mau.

parole.significato: a delimited piece of ground, e.g. a flowerbed
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch perc, from Old Dutch perk (attested in placenames), from Frankish *parrik, from Proto-Germanic *parrukaz. Compare also park and German Pferch.
From Middle Dutch pot, from Old Dutch *pot, from Frankish *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot”). Cognate with German Pott and English pot (“pot”).

parole.significato: a rat, medium-sized rodent belonging to the genus Rattus, or of certain other genera in the family Muridae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ratte, from Old Dutch *rato, *roto, from Frankish *ratt, *rato, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz (“rat”). Related to Old High German rato.

parole.significato: heron, waterbird of the family Ardeidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reiger, from Old Dutch heigero, from Frankish *hraigrō, from Proto-Germanic *hraigrô.

From Middle Dutch schalc, from Old Dutch skalk, from Frankish *skalk, from Proto-Germanic *skalkaz (“servant, knight”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cleave, separate, part, divide”). Cognate to English shalk, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌻𐌺𐍃 (skalks).

parole.significato: a paddle, a blade of a water wheel or similar contraption
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schoepe, from Frankish *skopa, from Proto-Germanic *skōpōną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to cut, to scrape, to hack”).
From Middle Dutch schuum, schum, scum, from Old Dutch *skūm, from Frankish *skūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz. Cognate with German Schaum, English scum.

parole.significato: spruce; certain tree of the family Pinaceae, especially of the genus Picea, but also used for trees of the genera Abies…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sparre (“pole, beam”), from Old Dutch *sparro, from Frankish *sparro, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô. Cognate to West Frisian spjir.
From Middle Dutch spene, from Old Dutch *speno, from Frankish *spenō, from Proto-Germanic *spenô (“nipple”).
From Middle Dutch spreiden, from Old Dutch *spreiden, from Frankish *spraidijan, from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną.

parole.significato: to strike, go on a strike
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch staken, derived from stake (“thin pole”), from Old Dutch *stako, from Frankish *stakō, from Proto-Germanic *stakô.
From Middle Dutch stoc, from Old Dutch stok, from Frankish *stokk, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz.
From Middle Dutch vāle, from Old Dutch *falo, from Frankish *falu, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz.
From Middle Dutch vaelde, vaelt, from Old Dutch *faled, from Frankish *falud (“pen for animals, fold”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *faludaz (“enclosure”).
From Middle Dutch vels (“rock, cliff”), from Old Dutch *felis, from Frankish *falis, from Proto-Germanic *falisaz.
From Middle Dutch visch, from Old Dutch fisc, from Proto-West Germanic *fisk, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.
From Middle Dutch wat, from Old Dutch *wada, from Frankish *wad, from earlier *wada (attested as Latinised acc. sg. vadam c. 108), from Proto-Germanic *wadą.

parole.significato: whale, mammal of the order Cetacea
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch walvisch, from Old Dutch walvisk, from *wal (“whale”), presumably to clarify the meaning. Equivalent to wal (“whale”) + vis (“fish”). Old Dutch *wal is from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”). See also waldier,

parole.significato: a mitten, type of glove in which four fingers get only one section, besides the thumb
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch want, from Old Dutch *want, from Frankish *wantu, from Proto-Germanic *wantuz.

parole.significato: to wager, to bet, to accept a gamble
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wedden, from Old Dutch *weddon, from Frankish *weddōn, *wadjōn, from Proto-Germanic *wadjōną. Cognate with Low German wedden, West Frisian wedzje, German wetten, English wed, Danish vædde, Icelandic veðja.
